FACULTY SENATE OFFICE F ACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION January 23, 2025 Gr aduate Council Report #2024-2025-04 The following matter was discussed and recommended by the Graduate Council at their November, 2024 meeting after similar legislation was advanced in a joint action by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) and the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) last November. Their intent was to ensure a streamlined curricular approval process for online undergraduate courses, regardless of their calendar format The Graduate Council now requests that the Faculty Senate approve the same measure for graduate-level courses. Con text: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions). Pr oposed: Any course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms. Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-09 Motion Regarding Honors Representation in the Faculty Senate March 6, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting MOTION - That the Honors Program gain representation in the Faculty Senate per the following: Over the last year, the Faculty Senate, through its standing and special committees, has worked with Honors to restructure the program, and continues to actively pursue an option that would create a University-Sponsored Institute to house Honors. Until such time as this Institute is created or Honors is otherwise restructured, it is important that the program be represented formally in the university’s shared governance structure. While the program is undergoing a significant transition, it seems prudent to have an Honors representative actively participating in meetings where the future of the program is being discussed. Analogous to the way that deans and other administrators serve as ex officio members of the Faculty Senate, i.e. without the right to vote, but with the right to make and second motions and participate in debate, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee proposes that that the Honors Program Director become an ex officio member of the Faculty Senate effective immediately. ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.

Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.
The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.

The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
